newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Exxon Valdez makes waves seven years after disaster.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Exxon Valdez makes waves seven years after disaster.

text.p: Seven years after the Exxon Valdez ploughed into the Alaskan coast spewing 35,000 tonnes of crude into the sea, the effects of the disaster are still being felt by the world's oil tanker fleet.

The biggest U.S. oil spill ever prompted tougher financial penalties for polluters, changed the way in which tankers are built and catapulted environmental concern about transporting oil into the political limelight.
In the United States the Oil Pollution Act 1990 (OPA 90) was passed to limit oil spills in U.S. waters, but its impact was to be global.

"The impact of Valdez and OPA 90 has been great and will be felt into the next century," said Roger Kohn at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), the United Nations body that covers maritime issues.
OPA 90 forced tanker operators, rather than governments, to shoulder the financial cost of clean up operations and compensation.
Owners are required to carry COFRs (Certificates of Financial Responsibility) if sailing to the United States, showing they can pay for any potential spill.

"Every tanker going to the States must have a contingency plan (in the event of a spill) and a contract with a local U.S. company that does oil spill clean up," said Svein Ringbakken at Intertanko, the independent tanker owners association.

The accident also prompted the implementation of contingency plans to clean up afterwards. Exxon came in for heavy criticism because of its initial slow response to the spill and problems of co-ordinating the clean-up.
"It (the Valdez) led to the adoption of a new international treaty on oil pollution preparedness response and co-operation (OPRC)," said Kohn.
OPRC laid down that clean-up equipment should be stockpiled and readily available, that trained personnel be on hand and that the IMO should act as co-ordinator in the event of a major spill.

Charterers in South Korea, a major importer of oil, now adhere to an unwritten rule to only fix modern tonnage, which overall tends to be safer than older ships, added Mark Jenkins, director of research at shipbrokers Simpson Spence and Young.
"There has been intense public pressure in Korea to serve the public interest by eliminating some of the risk by fixing modern ships," he said.
The Valdez heralded the arrival of tankers with double-hulls -- an inner skin of steel that holds the oil, a cavity buffer space, and then an outer skin.
Within 25 years all tankers will have a double-hull or similar design or face the scrapyard.
"All oil tankers, bar some Russian vessels, built after 1992 will have the double-hull configuration," said one shipping analyst.
The tanker industry cites a reduction in the amount of oil lost on voyages as proof that increased environmental concern in addition to legislation has been taken seriously.
The amount of oil lost through tanker mishaps has been steadily dropping over the last three decades. In the 1970s an average 311,400 tonnes of oil was spilt by tankers every year.

In the 1980s this fell to 118,000 tonnes and so far this decade an average of 88,000 tonnes has been spilt annually, according to figures from the International Tanker Owners Pollution Federation (ITOPF).

Intertanko, whose members control two thirds of the global tanker fleet, claim 99.9 percent of the 1,800 million tonnes of crude and petroleum products transported every year reach their destination safely. A single disaster like the Valdez, or the Sea Empress off the South Wales coast, dramatically lifts the average.
But there is not universal agreement on the issue.
The double hull design has come in for criticism and the focus of tanker accidents has been overplayed to the detriment of other areas of marine oil pollution, some industry observers said.
"The trouble with large tanker accidents is they make good headlines - the larger the spill the higher the profile," says John Harris, a senior consultant at Drewry Shipping Consultants.

This can mean that other problem areas fail to come out of the shadows, Harris said. Intertanko estimates nearly 95 percent of marine oil pollution arises from land-based and tanker's operational discharging.

Operational discharging, when a tanker cleans its tanks with sea water and empties the residue in the open sea, and land sourced industrial pollution are less photogenic and get less television air time, said Harris.

Double hulls, adopted globally from the commercial pressure to stay in tune with the U.S. are seen by some designers to be better suited to the sandy, gently sloping east coast of the US compared with the rocky shorelines of northern Europe.

If the outer skin is punctured water can rush in and weigh the tanker down, potentially on to rocks, making salvage harder. A double hull would not have protected the Exxon Valdez which was travelling at a speed that would have punctured both hulls.
Ship designers have come up with half a dozen alternative designs to the double hull, but none have been built.
